title: Who goes, who stays: allocating pieces to a plan
outcomes: Counts the pieces that bear on the target, and those that can join, against the defenders
Names a piece that must stay home and says what it blocks or guards
Says when there is no definite target to allocate pieces to

steps.text: **Allocation** starts with a target: a king, a weak pawn. Decide where the main blow falls, which pieces can go, and which are the minimum to keep at home. *Rule of thumb:* keep the defenders that also do other work (a knight on f3 can guard the king's side and the centre), and do not send everything. With no target yet, there is nothing to allocate.

steps.caption: White to move. The knight on f3 looks ready to jump to g5. What else is it doing?

line.say: Black's bishop now attacks g2 and takes it.
Bxg5: the black bishop takes the knight.
fxg5 recaptures. Pieces are level, but White's bishop on g2 is gone and the engine rates Ng5 well below the best move.

claims.statement: Black does not attack g2 now.
Ng5 is at least 80 cp worse than the best move.

steps.title: Who stays, who goes
steps.prompt: Same position, three questions. First: which white man is already doing a defensive job? Second: does sending the knight to g5 work? The third is a different position: is there anything definite to allocate pieces to? Predict the last two, then check.

steps.text: A piece that looks like an attacker may be a defender: ask what changes if it leaves. Reserve only the necessary defenders, and recount, because one missed defender turns a winning attack into a losing one. *Rule of thumb:* count the pieces already aimed at the target plus those that can join with a threat next move; attack when that total beats the defenders. If not, improve your pieces first. The counting itself is taught in "Count before you attack: attack now, not yet, or no".

steps.prompt: Open one of your own games (My games) and pick a middlegame position where you attacked. Write down the allocation you used and the one you would use now.
